body.heading: Stress, stored like a bent stick
paragraphs: Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that drift a few centimetres a year. Along their edges, friction locks the rocks together even as the plates keep pushing. The rock bends and stores energy, the way a stick flexes further and further in your hands.

When the stress finally beats friction, the fault slips — sometimes by metres in seconds — and the stored energy radiates outward as seismic waves. That release point is the earthquake's focus; the spot on the surface above it is the epicentre.

body.heading: Reading the waves
paragraphs: Seismometers around the world record two main families of waves: fast compressional waves and slower shear waves. The gap between their arrivals at a station reveals how far away the quake struck, and combining three or more stations pinpoints it.

Earthquakes cannot yet be predicted in the way weather can, and honest seismologists say so plainly. What science can do is map the faults, measure the strain, and build structures that ride out the shaking when the ground lets go.

takeaway: Earthquakes release energy stored in stressed rock along faults, and their waves let scientists locate and measure them.
